intro/hello: This lecture is about reinforcement learning from human feedback, R L H F, and the algorithm that made it work: P P O.
intro/mimic: A pretrained language model is a superb mimic. It continues any text the way the internet would.
intro/moon: Ask it to explain the moon landing to a six year old, and it may answer with more questions just like yours.
intro/sft: Fine-tuning on written demonstrations teaches the format, but they are slow to write, and only show what to do.
intro/judge: People are much better at judging answers than at writing them. Which of these two is better? Anyone can tell.
intro/recipe: So R L H F collects comparisons, fits a reward model to predict them, and then trains the language model against that reward model.
intro/ppo: That last step is reinforcement learning, and the algorithm of choice was P P O: proximal policy optimization.
intro/plan: We will build each piece in turn, and then see how it all goes wrong.
recap/policy: First, a recap. The language model is a policy: each next token is an action, and when the answer is finished, a reward says how good it was.
recap/adv: The policy gradient pushes every token the model wrote in proportion to its advantage: how much better things went than expected.
recap/sign: Positive advantage: more likely next time. Negative: less likely.
recap/baseline: Subtracting a baseline leaves the average gradient unchanged, and makes it far less noisy.
recap/leash: And a frozen copy of the starting model, the reference, acts as a leash.
recap/kl: The K L divergence measures how far the policy has drifted, and the objective pays beta times that drift.
recap/why: Without it, the policy can wander into strange text that happens to score well. Hold that thought.
recipe/intro: The standard recipe comes from Instruct G P T, by Ouyang and colleagues at Open A I, in twenty twenty two. It has three stages.
recipe/sft: Stage one, supervised fine-tuning. Labelers write answers to about thirteen thousand prompts, and the pretrained model imitates them.
recipe/sample: Stage two. The fine-tuned model, called S F T, writes four to nine answers to each prompt.
recipe/rank: Labelers rank them, best to worst. Ranking is far quicker than writing.
recipe/rm: Those rankings train a reward model: a network that reads a prompt and an answer, and outputs a single number.
recipe/ppo: Stage three. A copy of the S F T model becomes the policy. It answers new prompts, the reward model scores them, and P P O updates it.
recipe/nohuman: In stage three, nobody writes or ranks anything. The reward model stands in for people: the power of the method, and its weak point.
recipe/result: People preferred a one point three billion parameter Instruct G P T to the hundred and seventy five billion parameter G P T 3. Chat G P T, later that year, used the same methods.
bt/scales: Why comparisons, and not scores? Ask ten people to rate an answer out of ten, and you get ten different scales.
bt/pairs: Ask which of two is better, and they agree much more often. So the data is triples: a prompt, a chosen answer, and a rejected one.
bt/rankings: A ranking of nine answers holds thirty six pairs.
bt/noise: Labels are still noisy: Instruct G P T's labelers agreed with each other about three quarters of the time.
bt/model: The reward model is a language model whose vocabulary output is swapped for a single number.
bt/bt: To connect scores to choices, we use the Bradley-Terry model, from nineteen fifty two: the chance of preferring the chosen answer is the sigmoid of the difference between the two scores.
bt/zero: A margin of zero is a coin flip.
bt/two: A margin of two means eighty eight percent. Only the difference matters, so adding a constant to every score changes nothing.
bt/loss: The loss is minus the log of that probability: logistic regression, where the right answer is always that the chosen one wins.
bt/grad: Its slope is steepest when the model has a pair backwards, so training concentrates on the pairs it gets wrong.
rmtoy/toy: Here is a toy where we can watch one learn. Each answer is a point with two features: its length, and its quality.
rmtoy/cloud: The fine-tuned model's answers form a cloud. Their length varies a lot, their quality only a little.
rmtoy/taste: Simulated labelers have a hidden taste: quality matters most, some extra length helps, and too much length hurts.
rmtoy/pairs: They compare pairs and pick winners, noisily. Each line joins a pair; the filled dot is the one they chose.
rmtoy/linear: Our reward model is linear: a weighted sum of length and quality. It starts out random, and gets most pairs backwards.
rmtoy/train: Training on the Bradley-Terry loss turns its contours until they agree with the labels...
rmtoy/ceiling: ...up to about seventy percent of new pairs: close to the ceiling set by the labelers' own noise.
rmtoy/curve: But look at the labelers' true taste. Its contours curve, because length helps only up to a point.
rmtoy/straight: A linear model can only draw straight lines, so it learns that longer is always better. Inside the cloud, that is nearly right. Remember it.
ratio/cost: Now, stage three. Its expensive part is generation: every batch means sampling whole answers from a large model, token by token.
ratio/once: Reinforce takes one gradient step on that batch, and throws it away. Why not take several?
ratio/stale: Because after one step, the batch is stale. It came from the old policy, and the gradient assumes samples from the current one.
ratio/is: Importance sampling fixes this. Weight each token by its ratio, rho: its probability now, over its probability when sampled.
ratio/double: A token that has become twice as likely counts twice, because the new policy would write it twice as often.
ratio/first: At the first step, every ratio is exactly one, and the gradient is exactly reinforce. After that, the ratios correct for the drift.
ratio/limit: But a dozen samples cannot say much about a policy far from the one that made them.
ratio/runs: Here are sixteen training runs on a prompt with five kinds of answer. With one step per batch, learning is steady, but slow.
ratio/twenty: With twenty steps per batch, the runs climb much faster. But some lurch onto a worse answer, and stay there.
ratio/stuck: Once an answer's probability is near zero, the policy stops sampling it, and never learns otherwise.
clip/trpo: P P O's predecessor, T R P O, said it directly: keep the new policy within a small K L distance of the old one, a trust region. Enforcing that takes heavy machinery.
clip/ppo: P P O, from twenty seventeen, gets most of the benefit with a small change to the loss.
clip/formula: For each token, take the ratio times the advantage, and the same with the ratio clipped into a narrow band. Keep the smaller one.
clip/eps: The band runs from one minus epsilon to one plus epsilon. Epsilon is usually zero point two, so from zero point eight to one point two.
clip/pos: Take a good token, with a positive advantage. As its ratio rises, the objective rises...
clip/flat: ...until one point two. Then the clipped term wins the minimum, and the curve goes flat. Once the token is twenty percent more likely, this batch stops asking for more.
clip/below: Below the band there is no clipping: if an update made a good token less likely, the full gradient pulls it back.
clip/neg: Now a bad token, with a negative advantage. Everything mirrors.
clip/negflat: Lowering its ratio helps until zero point eight. Then the curve goes flat.
clip/negabove: But if an update made a bad token more likely, there is no clipping. The full penalty applies.
clip/pessimism: That is what the minimum is for: clipping removes the incentive to keep improving, but never hides a step in the wrong direction.
clip/back: Back to our sixteen runs, now with clipping: still fast, and every run finds the best answer.
gae/credit: P P O needs an advantage for every token, but the reward model scores only the finished answer. Which tokens deserve the credit?
gae/value: The tool is a value head: at every position, a prediction of the reward still to come.
gae/delta: The prediction after a token, plus any reward that arrived, minus the prediction before it, is the surprise, delta. With a perfect value head, it equals the advantage on average.
gae/lam0: Trust the value head completely, and the advantage is just delta: low noise, but biased whenever the value head is wrong.
gae/lam1: Trust it only as a baseline, and the advantage is all the remaining reward minus the prediction: unbiased, but every later token adds noise.
gae/gae: Generalized advantage estimation blends the two. Each token adds up the surprises that follow it, weighted by lambda to the power of the distance.
gae/kernel: With lambda near zero, only the first surprise counts. With lambda near one, they all do.
gae/toy: Here is a ten token toy. Each token is good or bad, and the final reward counts the good ones, so good tokens truly deserve exactly one more than bad ones.
gae/flawed: Give it a flawed value head. At lambda zero, the estimates are tight, but the gap between good and bad tokens is far too small.
gae/one: At lambda one, the gap is right, but buried in noise.
gae/between: In between, lambda trades bias for variance. Language models usually take lambda around zero point nine five.
gae/vloss: The value head itself learns by plain regression onto the returns it sees, alongside the policy.
kl/chain: The K L leash has to work per token too. The log probability of an answer is the sum over its tokens.
kl/sample: So each written token's log ratio, policy over reference, estimates its share of the K L.
kl/fold: Implementations fold the penalty straight into the reward: every token pays beta times its log ratio.
kl/end: The reward model's score arrives only on the last token, and G A E spreads everything across the answer.
kl/sure: Here is one answer. The policy has learned to open with: Sure! The reference found that unlikely, so those two tokens carry most of the penalty.
kl/cheap: The tokens that actually describe the sea cost almost nothing.
kl/neg: One token's log ratio can even be negative. Averaged over many samples, though, it is the K L, which never is.
kl/beta: Raise beta, and drift costs more. Near zero point three, it eats almost everything the reward model gave.
models/four: Put it all together, and one P P O iteration touches four networks.
models/policy: The policy, which writes the answers, and is trained.
models/ref: The reference: a frozen copy of the S F T model, for the K L penalty.
models/rm: The reward model, also frozen, which scores each finished answer.
models/critic: And the value model, trained, which predicts the reward to come at every token.
models/bytes: Training a model with Adam in mixed precision costs about sixteen bytes per parameter. A frozen model costs two.
models/total: So a seven billion parameter policy with same-sized helpers needs about two hundred and fifty gigabytes before a single activation: more than twice what fine-tuning needs.
models/small: That is one reason Instruct G P T kept its reward and value models at six billion parameters, even for its largest policy.
models/loop: One iteration: generate a batch, score it, turn the scores into per-token rewards and advantages, then run several clipped epochs over it.
models/preview: Later recipes trim this. G R P O drops the value model. D P O drops both the reward model and the value model.
hacking/notlabelers: Now the catch. The reward model is not the labelers. It was fit to comparisons of S F T answers, and is only accurate where those answers lived.
hacking/optimizer: And the policy is an optimizer, pointed straight at it.
hacking/goodhart: Push hard enough, and it finds answers the reward model loves for the wrong reasons. Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
hacking/examples: Real models learned to write longer, to agree with the user, and to sound confident: reward, without being more correct.
hacking/toy: Back to our toy reward model. The policy is now a cloud of answers, and each step moves it toward a higher score, minus beta times the K L.
hacking/run: With a weak leash, the answers grow longer and longer, and the reward model's score climbs without end...
hacking/peak: ...while the labelers' true taste rises, peaks, and then collapses.
hacking/gao: Gao, Schulman and Hilton measured exactly this shape in twenty twenty two, with a large reward model standing in for people.
hacking/leash: With a stronger leash, beta near zero point three, the policy stops close to the peak.
hacking/hard: That is what beta is for, and why setting it is hard: in a real run, nobody can see the true curve.
hacking/fixes: So practitioners keep the K L penalty, pick checkpoints by human evaluation, and refresh the reward model with comparisons of the policy's own answers.
outro/recap1: To recap. R L H F learns a reward from human comparisons: a Bradley-Terry classifier on score differences.
outro/recap2: P P O reuses each expensive batch for several steps, weighting tokens by the ratio rho, and clips that ratio pessimistically, so no batch moves a token far.
outro/recap3: A value head and G A E turn one score per answer into an advantage per token, with lambda trading bias for variance.
outro/recap4: The K L penalty, paid token by token, keeps the policy near the reference, where the reward model can be trusted.
outro/recap5: And the learned reward is only a proxy. Optimize it too hard, and quality falls.
outro/next: Next come two simplifications: D P O, which skips the reward model and the sampling, and G R P O, which drops the value head.
